CNS07 · Pathology · Study Guide

Perinatal Disorders & CNS Malformations

Learning objectives

  1. LO 1Malformations: explain what neural tube defects and forebrain (induction) anomalies are, and where they sit among CNS malformations.
  2. LO 2Malformations: explain how myelomeningocele, holoprosencephaly, lissencephaly and cortical dysplasia develop, and recognize their gross and microscopic pathology.
  3. LO 3Malformations: connect a patient's clinical picture (prenatal screen, face, spine, seizures) to the malformation that causes it.
  4. LO 4Malformations: match each malformation to its chromosomal, single-gene and environmental causes.
  5. LO 5Malformations: predict prognosis and know the prevention and treatment options for each malformation.
  6. LO 6Perinatal injury (white matter necrosis, germinal matrix hemorrhage, multicystic encephalopathy): know who is at risk, how the injury happens, and what the brain looks like.
  7. LO 7Perinatal injury: connect a newborn's history and signs to the perinatal lesion behind them.
  8. LO 8Perinatal injury: recognize the (limited) genetic and molecular contributions to these mostly acquired injuries.
  9. LO 9Perinatal injury: predict the outcome and the short- and long-term complications of each lesion.

MAPBig picture

  • Malformation → the blueprint is wrong (≈5–10 / 1,000 births · mostly multifactorial)
  • Which step failed + when → which malformation
    • Tube closure → NTDs
    • Forebrain split → holoprosencephaly
    • Neuron migration → lissencephaly, polymicrogyria
    • Neuron organization → cortical dysplasia
  • Big defects → found prenatally (AFP, ultrasound) · subtle cortical defects → epilepsy, delay
  • Perinatal injury → normal brain damaged by hypoxia-ischemia → gestational age decides pattern
    • Preterm → germinal matrix hemorrhage · periventricular white matter necrosis
    • Late / term → multicystic encephalopathy
  • Malformation vs disruption → recurrence risk (genetic counseling)

LO 1Defining NTDs & forebrain anomaliesWhat goes wrong, where it fits, and the vocabulary you need first

By the end: you can define a neural tube defect and a forebrain-induction defect, place each on the developmental timeline, list the main malformation groups, and explain why "malformation" and "disruption" are not the same thing.
Q1. What is a "malformation" and how is it different from a disruption or deformation?

Malformation

  • A primary error in the embryonic/fetal developmental program itself.
  • Cause: genetic, environmental, or (most often) both.
  • Significant recurrence risk (only primary malformations carry it) → genetic counseling matters.

Disruption / deformation

  • An insult on a normal program → secondary damage.
  • Causes: vascular accident, necrosis from infection, compression / mechanical trauma.
  • Low recurrence risk.

Why is the distinction hard?

  1. Brain development is long: it continues after birth (myelination; late-migrating cerebellar granule cells).
  2. Timing changes the look: the same insult produces different morphology at different ages (selective vulnerability).
  3. Repair changes over time: macrophage responses appear well before astrocytes can react.
    • Early disruption → dead tissue is resorbed without glial repair → a smooth-walled hole/pore with no gliosis.
    • Late disruption → glial scar forms → looks more destructive.
  4. Limited repertoire: the brain can only react in a few ways, so one anomaly (e.g., polymicrogyria) can come from many causes, genetic or environmental.

How common, and how severe?

  • Birth prevalence: 5–10 per 1,000 births; CNS malformations are present in ≈15% of infants who die of birth-defect-related causes.
  • Spectrum of severity:
    • Gross defects that threaten life directly → anencephaly, myelomeningocele, encephalocele.
    • Subtle defects whose main consequences are epilepsy and intellectual disability → lissencephaly, polymicrogyria, cortical dysplasia, tuberous sclerosis.
    • Functional deficits → learning and behavior problems.
CheckA fetal brain shows a smooth-walled cavity with no glial scar. Early or late insult?
Early (before the brain can mount an astrocytic response). Macrophages cleaned up the dead tissue; there was no gliosis to leave a scar.
Memory tool

Blueprint vs. wrecking ball. Malformation = wrong blueprint (can be handed to the next child). Disruption = a wrecking ball hit a correctly built house (usually won't happen again).

Q2. How does the neural tube normally close, and what is a neural tube defect?
  • The neural tube is the precursor of the entire CNS. It forms when the neural folds fuse in the midline (primary neurulation).
  • Closure starts ≈day 22 after ovulation (closure site 1, cervical region), then at a second site, and zips both cranially and caudally.
  • Anterior neuropore closes ≈day 26; posterior neuropore ≈day 28.
  • Secondary neurulation (after primary closure): the lowest sacral cord and other non-epidermal tissues form from multipotent stem cells in the tail bud.
  • Neural tube defect (NTD) = dysraphic disorder: failure of the neural folds to close (primary or secondary neurulation), so the tube and its bony/skin coverings stay open or malformed.
CheckWhy does folic acid have to start before conception?
Because the tube closes by day 26–28 (week 4), often before a woman knows she is pregnant. Starting folate after a positive test is too late for the window that matters.
Step 1 HY — NTD basics
  • Open NTDs leak fetal α-fetoprotein (AFP) → ↑ AFP in amniotic fluid and maternal serum; ↑ acetylcholinesterase (AChE) in amniotic fluid confirms an open neural defect.
  • Folic acid: 0.4 mg/day for all women of reproductive age; 4 mg/day if a prior child had an NTD or the mother takes antiepileptics such as valproate.
  • Risk factors: low folate, valproate, carbamazepine, folate antagonists (methotrexate, trimethoprim), pregestational diabetes, obesity, hyperthermia, prior affected child.
Step 1 trap — the "neuropore" mix-up

Anterior neuropore = cranial end (brain) → anencephaly. Posterior neuropore = caudal end (spinal cord) → myelomeningocele. Don't flip them because "posterior" sounds like "back of the head".

Q3. What are the members of the NTD family, from mildest to most severe?
DefectWhat is wrongCluesAFP
Spina bifida occultaMildest; tail-bud (secondary neurulation) defect; bony arch gap; skin closedTuft of hair, sacral dimple/sinus, skin tag, attached lipoma; may have hydromyelia, diastematomyelia, tethered cordNormal
MeningoceleAbnormal axial mesoderm → bony defect; meninges only herniate into a CSF sac; cord and central canal stay closedSkin-covered sac; neurologically mildUsually normal (↑ if open)
MyelomeningoceleMost severe spinal NTD: failure of posterior neural tube closure + bony defect; meninges + cord in the sacLumbosacral; area medullovasculosa; Chiari II + hydrocephalus↑↑
EncephaloceleBrain ± meninges herniate through a cranial bony defect (cranial meningocele if meninges only)Usually occipital; skin ulceration, infection↑ if open
AnencephalyFailure of anterior neuropore; absent cranial vault; exposed brain degeneratesArea cerebrovasculosa; froglike face; polyhydramnios↑↑

CheckWhat is the single feature that separates a meningocele from a myelomeningocele?
Whether spinal cord / neural tissue is in the sac. Meningocele = meninges + CSF only (cord stays closed in the canal). Myelomeningocele = cord and roots herniate too.
Step 1 HY — Classic spine findings
  • Spina bifida occulta: failure of vertebral arch fusion, dura intact, usually at L5–S1; tuft of hair or dimple; normal AFP.
  • Anencephaly → maternal polyhydramnios (the fetus can't swallow).
  • Occipital encephalocele + polycystic kidneys + polydactyly = Meckel-Gruber syndrome (autosomal recessive ciliopathy).
Buzzwords
"tuft of hair over the low back" → spina bifida occulta "area cerebrovasculosa" → anencephaly "area medullovasculosa" → myelomeningocele "↑ AChE in amniotic fluid" → open NTD "froglike face, absent skull vault" → anencephaly
Q4. What is a "forebrain anomaly", and how are malformations grouped overall?
  • Disorders of forebrain induction = hemispheric anomalies from failed separation of the forebrain vesicles (prosencephalon → two hemispheres) and failed commissure development (corpus callosum).
  • Main example: holoprosencephaly (a disorder of forebrain induction/patterning; ventral midline signaling = Sonic hedgehog).
  • Forebrain separation happens in weeks 5–6, right after neural tube closure. The face forms at the same time from the same midline signals → face and forebrain fail together.
GroupMembersFailed step
Neural tube defects (dysraphic)Anencephaly, encephalocele, myelomeningocele, meningocele, spina bifida (occulta)Neurulation (wk 3–4)
Chiari malformationsChiari I, II, IIIPosterior fossa / hindbrain development
Disorders of forebrain inductionHoloprosencephalyProsencephalon cleavage (wk 5–6)
Neuronal migration disordersLissencephaly type I (agyria/pachygyria), polymicrogyria, heterotopia, focal cortical dysplasiaNeuron proliferation, migration, organization (≈wk 8–24)
OtherCerebellum, brainstem and cord malformations (e.g., Dandy-Walker); hydrocephalusVarious
  • Learn the malformation list by group, with a one-line definition for each: NTDs → Chiari → forebrain induction → neuronal migration → cerebellum/brainstem/cord → hydrocephalus.
CheckIs holoprosencephaly a neural tube defect?
No. The tube closes normally; the problem is that the forebrain fails to divide into two hemispheres. It is a disorder of forebrain induction, and AFP is not elevated.
Memory tool

"Close → Cleave → Climb → Construct." Tube closes (NTDs) → forebrain cleaves (holoprosencephaly) → neurons climb to the cortex (lissencephaly, heterotopia) → cortex is constructed into layers (polymicrogyria, FCD).

ApplyLO 1 application questions

A1A fetus is exposed to a teratogen on day 40 of development. Is an NTD likely? What forebrain process is still vulnerable?
An NTD is unlikely; forebrain cleavage and cortical development are still vulnerable. The neuropores closed by day 28. Day 40 falls during prosencephalon cleavage (≈wk 5–6) and before neuronal migration.
A2Two couples each have a child with polymicrogyria: one from a GPR56 mutation, one from congenital CMV. Which couple needs counseling about a high recurrence risk?
The GPR56 couple. That is a primary malformation (autosomal recessive → 25% recurrence). The CMV case is a disruption, and its recurrence risk is low. Same pattern, different causes, which is the brain's "limited repertoire".
A3A newborn has a skin-covered lumbar sac. MRI shows only CSF and meninges in the sac and a normally closed cord. Name it and predict the AFP.
Meningocele; AFP usually normal. No neural tissue in the sac, and the skin covers it, so fetal AFP doesn't leak.

LO 2Pathogenesis & pathologyMyelomeningocele, holoprosencephaly, lissencephaly, polymicrogyria and cortical dysplasia

By the end: for each key malformation you can say which step failed, describe the gross brain or spine, and recognize the histology (area medullovasculosa, 4-layer cortex, double cortex, dysmorphic neurons, balloon cells).
Q1. How does anencephaly form, and what does the specimen look like?
  • Mechanism: anterior neuropore fails to close → the cranial vault never forms over it → exposed neural tissue sits in neurotoxic amniotic fluid and degenerates.
  • Gross:
    • Absent/hypoplastic cranial vault and overlying tissue; brain replaced by a ragged, vascular mass = area cerebrovasculosa (disorganized vessels + neuroglial tissue).
    • Flat skull base, abnormal sphenoid, shallow orbits with protruding eyes, shallow sella turcica.
    • Absent hypothalamus and neurohypophysis.
    • Somatic associations: adrenal hypoplasia (no ACTH drive), large thymus, pulmonary hypoplasia.
  • Epidemiology: the most common congenital brain malformation in human fetuses; F > M; sporadic or familial; ≈10× more common in Wales and Ireland (≈1–6 per 1,000) than in the US (0.5–2 per 1,000); ↑ maternal serum AFP.
  • Outcome: incompatible with prolonged life after birth.
CheckWhy are the adrenals small in anencephaly?
No hypothalamus/pituitary axis → no fetal ACTH → the fetal adrenal cortex is not stimulated and stays hypoplastic.
Q2. What is the pathology of a myelomeningocele?
Failureposterior neuropore doesn't close
→
Bony defectlarge vertebral arch gap
→
Herniationmeninges + spinal cord into a sac
→
Open cordflat, vascular plate = area medullovasculosa
  • Definition: the most severe spinal NTD, because both meninges and cord herniate (meningocele = meninges only).
  • Location: lumbosacral most common, usually solitary, ≈equal sex ratio. Lesions above T12 → female predominance and more malformations elsewhere.
  • Gross: fluctuant CSF-filled mass covered by skin or a thin membrane; dilated central canal; the posterior cord is open and blends with skin; nerve roots end blindly in the skin; at the defect the cord is a flat, highly vascular plate = area medullovasculosa (epithelializes after birth).
  • Micro: islands of disorganized neural tissue (neurons, glia) packed with dilated, thin-walled vessels, next to squamous epithelium.
  • Associations: Chiari II in >95%, plus hydrocephalus.
CheckArea cerebrovasculosa vs area medullovasculosa: which goes with which?
Cerebro = brain = anencephaly. Medullo = spinal medulla (cord) = myelomeningocele. Both are open, vascular, disorganized neural tissue.
Step 1 trap

"Spina bifida" on Step 1 can mean either occulta (normal AFP, asymptomatic) or cystica (meningocele / myelomeningocele). Read for skin (intact vs open) and neuro deficits (none vs leg weakness, neurogenic bladder).

Q3. How does holoprosencephaly form, and how do its three forms look?
  • Mechanism: failure of the forebrain (prosencephalon) to cleave into two hemispheres; ventral midline patterning signal (SHH) is weak or absent.
  • A spectrum: alobar (worst) → semilobar → lobar (mildest). All forms lack a corpus callosum.
FormBrainFace
Alobar (most severe)Very small, helmet-shaped holosphere not divided into hemispheres; single monoventricle with a thin dorsal membrane; absent olfactory bulbs and hypophysis; no corpus callosum, no septum pellucidum; fused basal ganglia/thalami; hippocampal formation rims the ventricle; bizarre, radiating gyral pattern. Cerebellum keeps two hemispheres.Cyclopia (fused orbits/eyes), proboscis (ethmocephaly), cebocephaly (flat nose, single nostril), hypotelorism, microphthalmia, agnathia
SemilobarShallow interhemispheric fissure (posteriorly); no corpus callosum; cortex continuous across the midline frontallyHypotelorism, midline cleft lip/palate
Lobar (mildest)Hemispheres mostly separate; no corpus callosum; cortex continuous across the midline at the frontal pole/orbital surfaceMild hypotelorism, single central incisor
CheckWhich structure is absent in every form of holoprosencephaly?
The corpus callosum (the commissure can't form across a midline that never separated properly).
Step 1 HY — Holoprosencephaly
  • Ultrasound/MRI: single ventricle + fused thalami.
  • Causes: SHH mutation, trisomy 13 (Patau), maternal diabetes, fetal alcohol, Smith-Lemli-Opitz (cholesterol synthesis defect; SHH needs cholesterol).
  • Patau triad to recognize alongside it: holoprosencephaly, cleft lip/palate, postaxial polydactyly, rocker-bottom feet, cutis aplasia.
Memory tool

"The face predicts the brain." Cyclops eye → alobar. One front tooth → lobar. Read the face like a severity dial.

Q4. How do neurons build the cortex, and what is lissencephaly?
  • Neurons are born near the ventricles and migrate outward along radial glia to build a 6-layer cortex (inside-out: deep layers first). Migration depends on microtubule machinery (LIS1/dynein, doublecortin) and stop signals (reelin).
  • Neuronal migration disorders: gyri are too few, too many, too big or too small, and neurons are not where they belong.
  • Vocabulary: lissencephaly = "smooth brain" (term borrowed from lower animals); agyria = no gyri; pachygyria = few, broad gyri. A spectrum from totally smooth to focal smooth areas to large, simplified gyri.
  • Lissencephaly type I (classic):
    • Gross: smooth surface, open operculum (Sylvian fissure not covered), malformed gyri in a radial pattern.
    • Coronal: markedly thick cortex, thin white matter.
    • Micro: 4-layer cortex: molecular layer → thin outer neuronal layer → thin cell-sparse (white matter) layer → thick deep neuronal layer of neurons that never finished migrating.
CheckWhy is the cortex thicker in a "smooth" lissencephalic brain?
The neurons are all still there; they just piled up in a thick, deep layer instead of spreading into a folded 6-layer sheet. Less folding + same neuron number → thick cortex, thin white matter.
Step 1 trap — gyri

Pachygyria = few, broad gyri (pachy = thick). Polymicrogyria = many, small gyri. Opposite surfaces, both migration/organization disorders. Lissencephaly type II (cobblestone) is a different disease (over-migration through a broken pial surface; e.g., FCMD/fukutin).

Q5. What does polymicrogyria look like?
  • Many small, malformed convolutions: "gyri on gyri", a cobblestone / Morocco-leather surface. Underneath, the cortex is thin and abnormally layered (often 4-layered or unlayered), with fused molecular layers between microgyri.
  • Patterns: diffuse; symmetric in arterial territories; at the margins of pores (schizencephaly/porencephaly); focal anywhere; perisylvian/opercular; symmetric parietal and insular.
  • The "arterial territory" and "pore margin" patterns hint at a disruptive (ischemic or infectious) cause during mid-gestation.
Buzzwords
"smooth brain, open operculum" → lissencephaly type I "4-layered cortex" → classic lissencephaly "double cortex" → subcortical band heterotopia (DCX) "gyri on gyri / Morocco leather" → polymicrogyria "helmet-shaped holosphere" → alobar holoprosencephaly
Q6. What is focal cortical dysplasia (FCD), and how does it relate to tubers and hemimegalencephaly?
  • Malformations of cortical development result from abnormal proliferation, migration and differentiation of neurons and glia.
  • FCD = a focal patch of cortex with loss of normal lamination + large neurons in abnormal locations.
    • Dysmorphic neurons: enlarged, abnormally rotated or inverted, tortuous dendrites, clumped Nissl substance; inclusions can stain with Luxol fast blue (blue aggregates) and may even be GFAP-positive (a glial marker inside a neuron).
    • Balloon cells: large cells with glassy eosinophilic cytoplasm and an eccentric (peripheral) nucleus; some show membranous CD34 (stem-cell marker) staining → they are immature, mixed neuron/glia cells.
  • Normal cortex vs FCD: FCD shows absence of lamination + large nerve cells in an abnormal location.
  • Histologically, FCD IIb ≈ cortical tuber ≈ hemimegalencephaly.
LesionHistologyExtentClinical
FCD type IIaDysmorphic neurons, dyslamination, no balloon cellsFocalChildhood epilepsy
FCD type IIbDysmorphic neurons + balloon cellsFocalDrug-resistant focal epilepsy; resection
Cortical tuber (tuberous sclerosis)Same as FCD IIb + calcification, bizarre giant cellsMultiple firm, potato-like cortical thickenings; blurred grey–white junctionSeizures, ID; resect only if driving epilepsy
HemimegalencephalyFCD-type histologyWhole enlarged hemisphereContinuous, drug-resistant seizures from infancy
CheckA resected seizure focus shows dysmorphic neurons and balloon cells. The child has no skin lesions and no family history. FCD IIb or a tuber?
Histology can't separate them; context does. A single lesion with no other tuberous sclerosis features → FCD IIb. Multiple tubers + skin/cardiac/renal lesions or a TSC1/TSC2 variant → tuberous sclerosis.
Step 1 HY — Tuberous sclerosis
  • AD; TSC1 (hamartin, chr 9) or TSC2 (tuberin, chr 16) → loss of mTOR inhibition.
  • Brain: cortical tubers, subependymal nodules ("candle guttering"), SEGA (can block the foramen of Monro → hydrocephalus).
  • Skin: ash-leaf spots, facial angiofibromas, shagreen patch, periungual fibromas. Other: cardiac rhabdomyoma, renal angiomyolipoma, pulmonary LAM.
  • Infantile spasms → vigabatrin; SEGA/angiomyolipoma → everolimus (mTOR inhibitor).
Memory tool

Balloon = "blown-up glass": big, glassy pink cytoplasm with the nucleus pushed to the edge, like the knot at the end of a balloon.

ApplyLO 2 application questions

A1Biopsy from the flat red surface of a newborn's lumbosacral lesion shows disorganized glia and neurons with many dilated vessels beside squamous epithelium. Name the tissue and the defect.
Area medullovasculosa → myelomeningocele. The open, flattened cord is replaced by a vascular neuroglial plate that blends with skin.
A2An MRI shows a smooth brain whose malformation is worst in the parieto-occipital lobes, with a thick cortex. Predict the histology.
Classic 4-layer cortex (molecular, thin outer neurons, cell-sparse layer, thick deep neuronal layer): LIS1-type lissencephaly (posterior-predominant).
A3A fetal brain at autopsy is small and undivided, with one ventricle, fused thalami and no olfactory bulbs. What else will the pituitary show?
Absent (or hypoplastic) hypophysis. Alobar holoprosencephaly lacks olfactory bulbs and pituitary → risk of hypopituitarism and diabetes insipidus in survivors.
A4Predict what a CD34 stain highlights in FCD IIb, and what that tells you about the cell.
Membranous staining of some balloon cells: these are immature, progenitor-like cells that failed to differentiate properly.

LO 3Clinical ↔ pathologic correlationFrom screen, face, spine and seizures back to the lesion

By the end: you can read a vignette (MSAFP, ultrasound, facial features, spinal level, seizures, posterior fossa findings) and name the malformation, including Chiari I vs II vs Dandy-Walker and the hydrocephalus type.
Q1. How are NTDs picked up during pregnancy, and what does the newborn look like?
16–18 wkmaternal serum AFP screen (quad screen)
→
↑ AFPfetal ultrasound / MRI
→
Confirmamniotic AFP + acetylcholinesterase
→
Planin-utero repair or delivery planning
  • Anencephaly: diagnosed in utero; ↑ AFP; polyhydramnios; often ↓ fetal movement; absent vault and protruding eyes at birth.
  • Myelomeningocele: diagnosed in utero; deficits depend on lesion level (motor and sensory loss below it); loss of sacral innervation → bladder and bowel incontinence; lower-limb deformities (club feet).
  • Encephalocele: mass at the back of the skull, often ulcerated/infected; contains loose connective tissue, disorganized glia ± cortex and choroid plexus.
  • Occult spina bifida: asymptomatic or later tethered cord (back pain, leg weakness, bladder trouble during growth spurts).
CheckName three reasons MSAFP is high besides an open NTD.
Wrong dates (pregnancy further along than thought), multiple gestation, abdominal wall defects (gastroschisis, omphalocele); also fetal demise. Low AFP suggests trisomy 21.
Step 1 HY — Screening
  • ↑ AFP: open NTD, abdominal wall defect, multiple gestation, wrong dates. ↓ AFP: Down syndrome (with ↑ hCG, ↑ inhibin A, ↓ estriol).
  • Prenatal ultrasound signs of myelomeningocele + Chiari II: "lemon sign" (scalloped frontal bones) and "banana sign" (cerebellum wrapped around the brainstem).
Step 1 trap

A question that pairs ↑ MSAFP with "maternal diabetes" or "↑ HbA1c" usually wants the NTD, not diabetes. Pregestational diabetes does raise NTD risk, but its signature CNS anomalies are caudal regression and holoprosencephaly. Answer the lab question with ↑ AFP / ↑ AChE.

Q2. How do you tell Chiari I, Chiari II and Dandy-Walker apart?
FeatureChiari IChiari II (Arnold-Chiari)Dandy-Walker
What's wrongCerebellar tonsils herniate >3–5 mm below the foramen magnumSmall posterior fossa; vermis + tonsils + elongated medulla pushed through the foramen magnum; tectal beakingAbsent/hypoplastic vermis + cystic 4th ventricle filling an enlarged posterior fossa
AgeAdolescent / adultInfant (prenatal)Infant
Key associationSyringomyelia (cervical), occipital headache, cerebellar signsLumbosacral myelomeningocele (>95%), hydrocephalus (aqueductal stenosis), hydromyeliaHydrocephalus; other malformations
SeverityOften mild or asymptomaticSevere: brainstem dysfunction (stridor, apnea, swallowing)Variable
Posterior fossa sizeNormal/smallSmallLarge
  • Chiari III: rare; hindbrain (cerebellum ± brainstem) herniates through a low occipital/high cervical encephalocele.
CheckPosterior fossa is enlarged, vermis absent, big cyst in place of the 4th ventricle. Chiari II?
No: Dandy-Walker. Chiari II has a small posterior fossa crammed with herniating tissue; Dandy-Walker has a big one with a cyst.
Step 1 HY — Syrinx localization

A cervical syrinx (Chiari I) expands the central canal and first destroys the anterior white commissure (crossing spinothalamic fibers) → bilateral, cape-like loss of pain and temperature over the shoulders and arms with preserved vibration/proprioception. Expansion into the anterior horns → LMN wasting of the hands; lateral columns → UMN signs in the legs.

Memory tool

Chiari "1, 2" counts the structures: Chiari 1 → 1 structure (tonsils). Chiari 2 → 2+ structures (vermis + medulla) and 2 companions (myelomeningocele + hydrocephalus). Dandy-Walker = Dilated 4th ventricle, Without a vermis.

Buzzwords
"cape-like loss of pain/temp" → syringomyelia ± Chiari I "tectal beaking" → Chiari II "lemon + banana sign" → myelomeningocele with Chiari II "cystic 4th ventricle, absent vermis" → Dandy-Walker
Q3. Hydrocephalus: which type goes with which lesion?

CSF path: lateral ventricles → foramina of Monro → 3rd ventricle → cerebral aqueduct → 4th ventricle → foramina of Luschka (lateral) and Magendie (median) → subarachnoid space → arachnoid granulations → dural venous sinus.

Non-communicating (obstructive)

Block inside the ventricular system. Ventricles dilate upstream of the block.

e.g., aqueductal stenosis in Chiari II; Dandy-Walker; clot in the aqueduct after germinal matrix hemorrhage; SEGA at Monro.

Communicating

↓ CSF absorption at arachnoid granulations; all ventricles dilate.

e.g., scarring after hemorrhage or meningitis.

Hydrocephalus ex vacuo

Ventricles look big because brain tissue was lost, not because CSF is trapped. Normal pressure.

e.g., multicystic encephalopathy, atrophy.

  • In infants (open sutures) hydrocephalus → enlarging head circumference, bulging fontanelle, splayed sutures, "sunset eyes" (upward-gaze palsy from pressure on the dorsal midbrain).
CheckLateral + 3rd ventricles enlarged, 4th normal. Where is the block?
At the cerebral aqueduct (between the 3rd and 4th ventricles): non-communicating hydrocephalus, the Chiari II pattern.
Step 1 trap

Big ventricles + small brain / microcephaly = ex vacuo, not obstructive. Don't shunt a brain that's simply missing tissue.

Q4. How do holoprosencephaly and cortical malformations present clinically?

Holoprosencephaly

  • Diagnosed by fetal ultrasound (single ventricle, fused thalami).
  • Some stillborn. Liveborn: facial dysmorphism, psychomotor retardation, spasticity, seizures, apnea, disturbed temperature regulation (hypothalamus), endocrine deficits.
  • "The face predicts the brain."

Malformations of cortical development

  • Present with epilepsy in early childhood ± neurodevelopmental delay.
  • Unlike NTDs and holoprosencephaly, usually not diagnosed in utero.
  • Range from incidental to lethal; seizures and psychomotor retardation are typical.
  • Hemimegalencephaly: seizures are continuous and not stimulus-triggered, resistant to drugs.
  • Prenatal diagnosis: NTDs and holoprosencephaly. Cortical malformations → early-childhood epilepsy, not seen in utero.
  • Myelomeningocele → Chiari II (>95%) + hydrocephalus; the level of the lesion predicts function (see LO 5).
CheckWhy would an infant with alobar holoprosencephaly have unstable body temperature?
The midline hypothalamus is malformed (and the hypophysis is absent), so central thermoregulation and pituitary control fail.

ApplyLO 3 application questions

A1A 16-year-old has occipital headaches worse with coughing and lost pain/temperature sensation over both shoulders but feels a tuning fork normally. MRI?
Chiari I with a cervical syrinx. Tonsils below the foramen magnum (cough headache) + central cord lesion hitting the anterior white commissure.
A2A newborn with a lumbosacral open sac develops stridor and apnea in the first weeks. Explain.
Chiari II brainstem compression: the medulla and lower cranial nerves (vagus) are stretched/compressed through the foramen magnum → vocal cord paralysis, apnea, swallowing problems.
A3A 3-year-old has frequent focal seizures despite three drugs. MRI shows a blurred grey–white junction in one frontal gyrus; skin is normal. Most likely lesion?
Focal cortical dysplasia (type II). Single focal lesion, drug-resistant epilepsy, no tuberous sclerosis stigmata.
A4An 18-week ultrasound shows one ventricle and fused thalami; the fetus also has polydactyly and cleft lip. Name the brain lesion and the karyotype to check.
Holoprosencephaly; trisomy 13 (Patau).

LO 4Molecular & genetic findingsChromosomes, single genes and teratogens

By the end: you can name the chromosome or gene behind each malformation (trisomy 13, SHH, LIS1, DCX, RELN, ARX, FLNA, TSC1/2) and list the environmental causes.
Q1. Which chromosomal abnormalities cause CNS malformations?
AbnormalityCNS malformationOther clues
5p− (cri-du-chat)MicrocephalyHigh-pitched cat-like cry, ID
Trisomy 13 (Patau)HoloprosencephalyCleft lip/palate, postaxial polydactyly, microphthalmia, cutis aplasia
Trisomy 18 (Edwards)MicrocephalyClenched overlapping fingers, rocker-bottom feet, micrognathia
Trisomy 21 (Down)MicrocephalyFlat facies, single palmar crease; early Alzheimer

CheckWhich trisomy is most often linked to holoprosencephaly?
Trisomy 13 (most frequent chromosomal aberration in holoprosencephaly; trisomy 18 and triploidy are less common).
Q2. Which single genes should you link to which malformation?
Gene (protein)InheritanceMalformation / syndrome
SHH (sonic hedgehog, 7q36)AD (variable)Holoprosencephaly (HPE3); also SIX3 (2p21, homeobox), ZIC2 (13q32)
LIS1 = PAFAH1B1 (17p13.3)AD (deletion)Lissencephaly type I, posterior-predominant; encodes the non-catalytic subunit of platelet-activating factor acetylhydrolase; with neighboring genes → Miller-Dieker
DCX (doublecortin, Xq22)X-linkedMales: lissencephaly, anterior-predominant (± agenesis of corpus callosum). Females: subcortical band heterotopia
RELN (reelin, 7q22)ARLissencephaly + cerebellar and hippocampal hypoplasia (ataxia, ID, seizures)
ARX (X)X-linkedMale lissencephaly + ambiguous genitalia, corpus callosum agenesis, severe seizures, temperature dysregulation
FLNA (filamin A)X-linkedPeriventricular nodular heterotopia with epilepsy
FCMD (fukutin)ARLissencephaly type II (cobblestone), polymicrogyria; Fukuyama congenital muscular dystrophy
GPR56ARBilateral frontoparietal polymicrogyria
KAL1 (anosmin)X-linkedAbsent olfactory bulbs + no GnRH neurons → Kallmann syndrome
PAX6ADAniridia; homozygotes → severe neuronal migration disorder
UBE3AImprinting (maternal)Microcephaly, cerebellar atrophy → Angelman syndrome
TSC1/TSC2ADCortical tubers, subependymal nodules, SEGA (tuberous sclerosis)

  • Miller-Dieker = LIS1 + adjacent genes → microcephaly, bitemporal hollowing, small jaw, profound mental/motor retardation, feeding problems; early hypotonia → later hypertonia and seizures.
  • Holoprosencephaly chromosomes: half have a normal karyotype; trisomy 13 is the most frequent abnormality.
    • Genes: SHH (7q36), SIX3 (2p21), ZIC2 (13q32).
    • Deletions: del(18p), del(7q36), del(2p21), del(13q32), del(21q22.3); duplication dup(3p24-pter).
CheckA boy has anterior-predominant lissencephaly; his mother has epilepsy and an MRI "double cortex". Gene?
DCX (doublecortin), X-linked. Affected male = full lissencephaly; carrier female = band heterotopia (random X-inactivation gives two neuron populations: one migrates, one stalls).
Memory tool

LIS1 Lies in the back, DCX Drives in front. LIS1 → posterior smooth brain; DCX → anterior. And DCX = "Double Cortex X-linked".

Step 1 trap

Kallmann (anosmia + hypogonadotropic hypogonadism) is a neuronal migration problem (GnRH neurons fail to migrate from the olfactory placode), not a pituitary tumor. And Angelman (UBE3A, maternal) vs Prader-Willi (paternal deletion) at 15q11-13: don't flip the parent.

Q3. Which environmental factors cause CNS malformations?

Drugs

  • Valproic acid, carbamazepine → NTDs
  • Phenytoin
  • Retinoids (isotretinoin)
  • Warfarin
  • Thalidomide
  • Alcohol → microcephaly, HPE spectrum

Infections (TORCH)

  • CMV (periventricular calcification, polymicrogyria)
  • HSV, rubella
  • Toxoplasma (diffuse calcification)
  • Syphilis

Physical / maternal

  • X-radiation → microcephaly
  • Hyperthermia (fever, hot tubs) → NTDs
  • Maternal diabetes → HPE, caudal regression, NTDs
  • Folate deficiency → NTDs
  • Animal clue: lambs of ewes grazing on Veratrum californicum develop cyclopia → the plant alkaloid cyclopamine blocks SHH signaling (Smoothened).
CheckWhy do both a cholesterol-synthesis defect and cyclopamine cause holoprosencephaly?
Both cripple Sonic hedgehog signaling: SHH needs cholesterol modification to work (Smith-Lemli-Opitz), and cyclopamine blocks Smoothened, the downstream SHH transducer.
Step 1 HY — Teratogens
  • Valproate: ↓ folate absorption/metabolism → NTDs (≈1–2%); carbamazepine also (≈0.5–1%).
  • Methotrexate, trimethoprim: folate antagonists → NTDs.
  • Maternal diabetes: caudal regression syndrome (sacral agenesis), cardiac defects, NTDs, holoprosencephaly.
  • Fetal alcohol: microcephaly, smooth philtrum, thin upper lip; the leading preventable cause of ID.
Buzzwords
"bitemporal hollowing + smooth brain" → Miller-Dieker (17p13.3) "ambiguous genitalia + lissencephaly" → ARX "periventricular nodules of grey matter" → FLNA heterotopia "cyclopamine / Veratrum" → SHH → holoprosencephaly

ApplyLO 4 application questions

A1An infant has microcephaly, bitemporal hollowing, a small jaw, and a smooth brain most severe at the back. What test result do you expect?
Deletion at 17p13.3 including LIS1 and adjacent genes (FISH/microarray) → Miller-Dieker syndrome.
A2A woman with a single central incisor and mild hypotelorism has a baby with alobar holoprosencephaly. Which gene and what concept?
SHH (AD) with variable expressivity / incomplete penetrance: a mildly affected carrier parent (microform) can have a severely affected child.
A3A boy with lissencephaly, agenesis of the corpus callosum, ambiguous genitalia and temperature instability. Gene?
ARX (X-linked lissencephaly with abnormal genitalia).

LO 5Outcome & treatment of malformationsPrevention, surgery, shunts and seizure control

By the end: you can give the prognosis of each malformation, predict mobility from a myelomeningocele level, and name the prevention and treatment steps (folate, prenatal repair, shunt, epilepsy surgery, mTOR inhibitors).
Q1. How are neural tube defects prevented?
  • Cause is mostly unknown; familial in some cases, without a clear inheritance pattern.
  • Primary prevention: folic acid to mothers in the periconceptional period (introduced 1990; also grain fortification). It reduces but does not eliminate NTD risk.
  • Inositol may be a useful adjunct.
  • Mouse models: Splotch mice → anencephaly that is folate-preventable; curly tail mice → folate-resistant NTDs that are prevented by myo-inositol.
CheckWhat does the curly-tail mouse teach about folate-resistant NTDs?
Not all NTDs are folate-dependent; some respond to inositol instead. That's the rationale for inositol as an adjunct.
Q2. What is the outlook for each NTD, and how does myelomeningocele level predict walking?
DefectOutcomeTreatment
AnencephalyIncompatible with prolonged life: stillbirth or death within hours–daysNone (comfort care)
EncephaloceleDepends on size/contents; small ones compatible with lifeSurgical repair
MeningoceleCompatible with life; usually good functionSurgical correction
MyelomeningoceleSurvives; deficits set by level; hydrocephalus, Chiari II, neurogenic bladderIn-utero closure → better neurologic function + less shunting; otherwise early postnatal closure + VP shunt
OccultaUsually asymptomaticRelease of tethered cord if symptomatic
CheckA child with an L4 myelomeningocele: wheelchair, braces, or unaided?
Walks with braces / support devices (L3–L5 band). Expect bladder/bowel dysfunction too.
Step 1 HY — Living with myelomeningocele
  • Neurogenic bladder → clean intermittent catheterization, recurrent UTIs, risk of hydronephrosis.
  • Latex allergy (repeated surgical/catheter exposure): use latex-free equipment.
  • VP shunt complications: infection, malfunction (headache, vomiting, lethargy, ↑ head size).
  • Later tethered cord → new back pain, leg weakness, worsening bladder.
Step 1 trap

Sources differ on the unaided-walking cutoff ("below S1" vs "below S2"). The idea is what's tested: low sacral lesions walk, high lumbar/thoracic lesions don't.

Q3. What happens to children with holoprosencephaly and cortical malformations?

Holoprosencephaly

Alobar: stillbirth or early death. Survivors: severe developmental delay, spasticity, seizures, apnea, temperature instability, pituitary deficits (diabetes insipidus). Lobar can be mild.

Tx: supportive; hormone replacement; feeding support.

Lissencephaly / Miller-Dieker

Profound ID and motor delay; infantile spasms and intractable epilepsy; feeding problems/aspiration; many die in childhood.

Tx: antiseizure drugs, gastrostomy, supportive.

Polymicrogyria

Seizures, ID, swallowing problems (bilateral perisylvian → pseudobulbar palsy), spasticity; varies with extent.

FCD & hemimegalencephaly

Drug-resistant epilepsy + developmental delay.

Tx: surgical resection of the FCD focus (often seizure-free); hemispherectomy for hemimegalencephaly.

Tuberous sclerosis

Epilepsy, ID, autism; SEGA → hydrocephalus.

Tx: tubers resected only if they drive epilepsy; vigabatrin for infantile spasms; everolimus for SEGA.

CheckWhy is surgery a realistic cure for FCD but not for lissencephaly?
FCD is focal: remove the patch, remove the seizure generator. Lissencephaly is diffuse: the whole cortex is abnormal, so there's nothing focal to resect.
Memory tool

"Focal → knife; diffuse → drugs and support."

ApplyLO 5 application questions

A1A woman with epilepsy on valproate wants to get pregnant next year. Two prevention steps?
Switch, if possible, to a safer antiseizure drug (e.g., lamotrigine or levetiracetam) before conception, and start high-dose folic acid (≈4 mg/day) before conception. Valproate carries the highest NTD and neurodevelopmental risk.
A2A 6-year-old with a repaired myelomeningocele and VP shunt has 2 days of headache, vomiting and sleepiness. First concern?
Shunt malfunction (obstruction) → raised ICP. Needs urgent imaging and neurosurgery.
A3A child with myelomeningocele has a severe reaction during surgery after the surgeon puts on gloves. Why?
Latex allergy (type I hypersensitivity) from repeated early latex exposure; these children need latex-free care.

LO 6Perinatal injury: risk, mechanism, pathologyGerminal matrix hemorrhage, white matter necrosis (PVL), multicystic encephalopathy

By the end: you can define the perinatal period, trace asphyxia to brain injury, list maternal/placental/fetal causes, and describe the risk factors, mechanism, gross and micro pathology of each of the three lesions.
Q1. What is perinatal brain injury, and how does asphyxia damage the brain?
  • Perinatal period = 20 gestational weeks → 28 postnatal days: a critical window of brain growth.
  • Most injury comes from hypoxia and/or ischemia, especially intrapartum during prolonged or difficult labor.
  • Clinical "asphyxia" = hypoxemia + poor perfusion → CO₂ retention and acidosis.
  • Unlike malformations, the cause is usually clear and the brain was built normally.
Hypoxemia+ poor perfusion
→
AcidosisCO₂ retention
→
Metabolic cascadeenergy failure, glutamate, Ca²⁺, free radicals
→
Multi-organ injuryhypotension, hypoglycemia, coagulopathy
→
Developing braindamage pattern depends on age
SourceCauses of asphyxia (before, during or after delivery)
MaternalSevere antepartum hemorrhage, shock (abruption), cardiac arrest, anemia, hypertension/toxemia, diabetes, autoimmune disease, intrauterine infection, smoking, trauma
PlacentalInfarcts, hemorrhage, infection (villitis), short cord or long cord around the neck
FetalCongenital malformations (CNS, respiratory, neuromuscular, heart), metabolic disease
CheckClassify: tetralogy of Fallot · chronic villitis · placental abruption.
Tetralogy = fetal. Chronic villitis = placental. Abruption = maternal (shock/antepartum hemorrhage; also placental).
Memory tool

"Mom, Placenta, Baby": every asphyxia cause sits in one of three boxes. Run through all three when a vignette gives you a damaged newborn.

Q2. Why does gestational age decide which lesion you get?
  • Preterm (<32–34 wk): the germinal matrix is still present and fragile → hemorrhage; immature oligodendrocytes in periventricular white matter → PVL.
  • Third trimester / term: mature cortex and white matter → global ischemia causes multicystic encephalopathy (and watershed or basal ganglia patterns).
Q3. What is the germinal matrix, and why does it bleed?
  • Germinal matrix = part of the subventricular zone along the lateral ventricles (over the head of the caudate, caudothalamic groove) that produces immature neurons and glia; persists until ≈34 weeks.
  • The commonest site of origin of periventricular and intraventricular hemorrhage in preterm infants (= subependymal hemorrhage).

Why it bleeds

  • Highly cellular zone with anastomosing capillaries and no supporting stroma; very vascular.
  • Sits at the border zone of striate and thalamic arteries.
  • Drains into thin-walled venules (dilate progressively from 23 weeks; only thicken after 34 weeks).
  • Hypoxic stress → loss of autoregulation → over-perfusion → rupture of fragile vessels; blood-pressure swings (ventilation, resuscitation) push flow straight into them.
  • Poor hemostasis with excess fibrinolytic activity in the matrix.

Risk factors

  • Gestational age at birth = the most important determinant: ≈10% at 30 wk, ≈40% at 26 wk, >50% at 24 wk.
  • Most bleeds occur in the first 3–24 hours after birth; most often in infants ventilated for immature lungs; hypoxia/ischemia; blood-pressure fluctuation.
  • Late bleeds (>24 h): respiratory distress syndrome, vigorous resuscitation, hypoxemia, seizures, BP fluctuation.

Grades (extent of the bleed)

  • Grade 1: confined to the germinal matrix (subependymal).
  • Grade 2: intraventricular, ventricle not distended.
  • Grade 3: intraventricular + ventricular distension / hydrocephalus.
  • Grade 4: rupture into surrounding white matter (parenchymal).
CheckWhy does the risk fall sharply after 34 weeks?
The germinal matrix has involuted and its venules have thickened; the fragile, stroma-poor vascular bed is gone.
Step 1 HY — IVH of prematurity
  • Typically <32 weeks / <1,500 g, within the first 72 h; often silent → screening cranial ultrasound through the anterior fontanelle.
  • Symptomatic: bulging fontanelle, ↓ hematocrit, hypotension, apnea, seizures, altered tone.
  • Antenatal corticosteroids reduce IVH (and RDS); delayed cord clamping also helps.
  • Grade 4 is now understood as a periventricular hemorrhagic venous infarction (the clot obstructs medullary/terminal veins).
Step 1 trap

Grade 2 vs 3 hinges on one word: distension. Blood in the ventricle with normal size = 2; blood with dilated ventricles = 3. And a term baby with a bleed is not a germinal matrix bleed (the matrix is gone); think trauma, coagulopathy, vitamin K deficiency, or venous thrombosis.

Q4. What is periventricular leukomalacia (white matter necrosis)?
  • Definition: infarcts of the periventricular white matter in premature infants (≈24–32 weeks).
  • Mechanism:
    • Watershed: the periventricular white matter sits at the end-zone between long penetrating (ventriculopetal) arteries → most vulnerable when perfusion drops.
    • Preterm infants have poor cerebral autoregulation → hypotension = ischemia.
    • Pre-oligodendrocytes are exquisitely sensitive to glutamate excitotoxicity, free radicals and inflammatory cytokines (chorioamnionitis, sepsis).
  • Gross: chalky white-yellow plaques next to the lateral ventricles (often near the angles of the ventricles); later cysts (cystic PVL), white matter loss, thin corpus callosum and ventriculomegaly.
  • Micro: coagulative necrosis, axonal swellings (spheroids), mineralization (calcium), lipid-laden macrophages, then reactive gliosis.
CheckWhich cell in the preterm white matter is the main victim?
The pre-oligodendrocyte (immature oligodendrocyte), the cell that should be myelinating → later ↓ myelin and white matter volume.
Step 1 HY — PVL

Preterm + periventricular white matter infarcts + chalky yellow foci with calcification → later spastic diplegia (legs > arms). Ultrasound: periventricular echodensities → cysts at 2–6 weeks.

Step 1 trap

CMV also gives periventricular lesions, but as periventricular calcifications with microcephaly, chorioretinitis and sensorineural deafness, not watershed infarcts after a hypotensive preemie course. Toxoplasmosis → diffuse (parenchymal) calcifications.

Q5. What is multicystic encephalopathy, and what does the brain look like?
  • Also called multicystic encephalomalacia / leukoencephalopathy.
  • When: later in gestation (3rd trimester), at or after birth; history of ↓ fetal movement or a co-twin dying in utero.
  • Mechanism: severe, global hypoxia-ischemia (trauma, placental failure, cardiac arrest, co-twin death) → liquefactive necrosis of cortex and white matter → macrophages clear debris → cysts.
  • Gross: "global hemispheric necrosis": small, light brain (e.g., 218 g vs normal 516 g at 2 months; 240 g vs 392 g at 16 days); multiple cysts in white matter and cortex; enlarged ventricles from tissue loss = hydrocephalus ex vacuo; a "spider's web" of fine gliovascular bands crossing the cavities.
  • Micro: loss of parenchyma, cavities, gliosis, calcium deposits, vascular dilatation.
FeatureGerminal matrix hemorrhagePVL (white matter necrosis)Multicystic encephalopathy
WhoPreterm, esp. <30 wk, ventilatedPreterm 24–32 wk3rd trimester / term / postnatal
MechanismFragile capillaries + loss of autoregulation + BP swings + fibrinolysisWatershed ischemia + inflammation → pre-oligodendrocyte deathSevere global hypoxia-ischemia → liquefactive necrosis
LocationSubependymal over caudate → ventricles → white matterPeriventricular white matterCortex + white matter, both hemispheres
GrossClot in matrix/ventricle; dilated ventriclesChalky white-yellow foci → small cystsMultiple cysts, spider's web bands, ex-vacuo ventricles
MicroBlood, then hemosiderin, cystic cavityCoagulative necrosis, spheroids, calcificationCavities, gliosis, calcium, dilated vessels
Main sequelPost-hemorrhagic hydrocephalusSpastic diplegiaMicrocephaly, quadriplegia, epilepsy, early death
CheckWhy are the ventricles big in multicystic encephalopathy if nothing is blocking CSF?
Because the surrounding brain tissue has been destroyed; CSF fills the space = hydrocephalus ex vacuo.
Step 1 HY

Brain infarcts undergo liquefactive necrosis (high lipid, few structural proteins, abundant lysosomal enzymes) → cysts. Contrast coagulative necrosis in heart, kidney, spleen.

Buzzwords
"spider's web of gliovascular bands" → multicystic encephalopathy "co-twin died in utero" → multicystic encephalopathy in survivor "chalky yellow periventricular foci" → PVL "subependymal bleed over the caudate" → germinal matrix hemorrhage "brain weight half of normal" → global destruction

ApplyLO 6 application questions

A1Predict the most likely perinatal brain lesion in (a) a 25-week ventilated preemie on day 1 with sudden hypotension, (b) a term infant after a uterine rupture.
(a) Germinal matrix/intraventricular hemorrhage; (b) global term hypoxic-ischemic injury → multicystic encephalopathy if severe. Age decides the vulnerable structure.
A2A placenta shows chronic villitis and villous infarcts; the 36-week baby was limp and apneic at birth and died at 16 days. Predict the brain.
Multicystic encephalopathy: small brain, global necrosis, cysts crossed by gliovascular bands, ventricles enlarged ex vacuo. Placental insufficiency (placental cause) → chronic/acute global ischemia.
A3Why does fibrinolytic activity in the germinal matrix matter?
Excess fibrinolysis + poor hemostasis means a small capillary leak isn't sealed and can grow into an intraventricular or parenchymal bleed.

LO 7Perinatal injury: clinical ↔ pathologic correlationReading the newborn's history, signs and imaging

By the end: given a newborn's gestational age, history and signs, you can name the lesion and predict what imaging or autopsy will show.
Q1. What clinical clues point to each lesion?

Germinal matrix hemorrhage

History: preterm, ventilated, RDS, resuscitation, BP swings; first 3–24 h.

Signs: often silent; or sudden deterioration: bulging fontanelle, ↓ hematocrit, hypotension, apnea, seizures, hypotonia.

Imaging: cranial ultrasound → echogenic blood in the matrix/ventricles; later enlarging ventricles.

PVL

History: preterm 24–32 wk; hypotension, sepsis, chorioamnionitis.

Signs: often quiet in the NICU → stiff, scissoring legs and delayed walking by 1–2 years.

Imaging: periventricular echodensities → cysts; MRI: periventricular white matter loss, irregular ventricles.

Multicystic encephalopathy

History: ↓ fetal movement, co-twin death in utero, placental infarcts/villitis with late prenatal care (placental cause), congenital heart disease (fetal cause), low Apgar, apnea at birth.

Signs from birth: seizures, hypertonia, irritability, abnormal cry, microcephaly → death in weeks, months or years.

Imaging: global ischemic injury, cortical abnormalities, ex-vacuo ventricles.

CheckA baby with tetralogy of Fallot, low Apgar and apnea needs a G-tube and dies at 2 months; the brain weighs less than half of normal. Lesion?
Multicystic encephalopathy (fetal cause of asphyxia: congenital heart disease) with global hemispheric necrosis.
Step 1 trap — enlarged ventricles at follow-up
  • Preemie with an early bleed → big ventricles months later = post-hemorrhagic hydrocephalus (obstructive/communicating), often with ↑ head size.
  • Big ventricles + small head = ex vacuo (PVL, multicystic).
  • Kernicterus (bilirubin) stains the basal ganglia (globus pallidus, subthalamic nucleus) → choreoathetosis, gaze palsy, deafness; it doesn't scar the aqueduct.
  • Medulloblastoma blocks the 4th ventricle in older children, not 8-month-old former preemies.
Q2. How do you tell perinatal injury from a malformation in a child with seizures and developmental delay?
CluePoints to malformationPoints to perinatal injury
HistoryNormal pregnancy/birth; family history; consanguinityPrematurity, difficult labor, abruption, low Apgar, ventilation
ExamDysmorphic face, other organ anomaliesSigns began at/after a hypoxic event
PathologyWrong architecture (no gyri, extra gyri, heterotopia, no midline split)Destroyed normal architecture: cysts, gliosis, calcification, hemosiderin
RecurrenceMay recur (genetic counseling)Usually low
Step 1 HY — Cerebral palsy
  • Cerebral palsy = non-progressive motor (movement/posture) disorder from a lesion of the developing brain; often with ID, epilepsy, visual and hearing problems.
  • Biggest risk factor: prematurity (PVL, IVH). Others: perinatal asphyxia, infection, multiple gestation, kernicterus.
  • Types: spastic (most common; diplegia, hemiplegia, quadriplegia), dyskinetic (choreoathetosis; basal ganglia), ataxic (cerebellum).
  • Losing skills over time = not CP → think metabolic/neurodegenerative disease.
Memory tool

Malformation = "never built right." Injury = "built right, then broken." Look for the broken pieces (cysts, scar, calcium, iron) to call injury.

ApplyLO 7 application questions

A1A 27-week preemie had a stormy NICU course with sepsis. At 20 months she can't walk; legs are spastic and scissor; arms and speech are near normal. Lesion and MRI?
PVL → spastic diplegia. MRI: periventricular white matter loss, irregular enlarged lateral ventricles, thin corpus callosum.
A2A 26-week ventilated infant's hematocrit falls from 45% to 32% on day 1 and the fontanelle bulges. Bedside test and likely finding?
Cranial ultrasound → germinal matrix hemorrhage extending into the ventricles (grade 2–3).
A3One monochorionic twin dies at 33 weeks; the surviving twin is born with seizures and microcephaly. Lesion?
Multicystic encephalopathy: acute hypotension/ischemia in the survivor through shared placental vessels when the co-twin dies.

LO 8Perinatal injury: genetic & molecular linksMostly acquired, but genes can load the dice

By the end: you can say why perinatal brain injury is mainly not genetic, and name the ways genes and molecules still matter (fetal anomalies, vessel-wall genes, clotting tendency, excitotoxic cascade, and genetic mimics).
Q1. Are germinal matrix hemorrhage, PVL and multicystic encephalopathy genetic diseases?
  • Mostly no. They are acquired injuries driven by prematurity, hypoxia-ischemia, blood-pressure instability and infection/inflammation. There is no single "PVL gene". Unlike malformations, the etiology is clear (perinatal hypoxia-ischemia).
  • Genes enter indirectly:
    • Fetal genetic disease that causes asphyxia: congenital heart disease (e.g., tetralogy of Fallot, which can be part of 22q11.2 deletion), neuromuscular or metabolic disease, CNS malformations.
    • Vessel-wall genes: COL4A1/COL4A2 (type IV collagen of basement membranes) variants → fragile small vessels → fetal/neonatal intraventricular hemorrhage and porencephaly; can recur in families.
    • Thrombophilia (e.g., factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A) → placental thrombosis/infarcts and perinatal arterial stroke.
    • Maternal conditions with genetic components (diabetes, hypertension, autoimmune disease) → placental dysfunction.
  • Molecular mechanism (shared by all three): energy failure → glutamate excitotoxicity (NMDA/AMPA receptors) → Ca²⁺ overload → free radicals, cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α from infection) → cell death (necrosis and apoptosis). Pre-oligodendrocytes lack antioxidant defenses → PVL.
CheckTwo siblings, both term, both have intraventricular hemorrhage and porencephaly. What should you suspect?
A familial small-vessel disorder such as a COL4A1 variant: term IVH is unusual, and recurrence in siblings argues for a genetic cause.
Step 1 trap — HIE mimics

A "floppy, seizing newborn" is not always asphyxia. Inborn errors (nonketotic hyperglycinemia, pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy, mitochondrial disease, urea cycle defects) can look like HIE. Clues: no sentinel event, normal cord gases, consanguinity, worsening after feeds, high ammonia/lactate.

Step 1 HY — Excitotoxicity

Hypoxia → ATP failure → Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase fails → depolarization → glutamate release + ↓ reuptake → NMDA receptor Ca²⁺ influx → proteases, lipases, NO, free radicals → neuronal death. Most vulnerable neurons: hippocampus (CA1), Purkinje cells, neocortical layers 3, 5, 6. Red neurons (eosinophilic cytoplasm, pyknotic nuclei) appear 12–24 h after injury.

ApplyLO 8 application questions

A1Parents of a baby with multicystic encephalopathy after a placental abruption ask about risk in their next child. What's the counseling point?
Recurrence risk for the brain lesion itself is low: it is a disruption of a normally formed brain, not a malformation. Address modifiable maternal/placental risks (e.g., hypertension, smoking).
A2Why does chorioamnionitis raise the risk of PVL even without hypotension?
Fetal inflammatory cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α) and activated microglia directly injure pre-oligodendrocytes (free radicals, excitotoxicity).
A3A newborn with "HIE" had a normal labor and normal cord pH but seizures on day 2 after starting feeds, and ammonia is very high. Rethink?
Inborn error of metabolism (e.g., urea cycle defect), a genetic mimic of perinatal asphyxia.

LO 9Perinatal injury: outcomes & complicationsShort-term crises and long-term disability

By the end: you can predict the short- and long-term outcome of each perinatal lesion, explain why PVL spares the arms, and name the preventive/therapeutic measures.
Q1. What happens after a germinal matrix hemorrhage?

Grade 1–2

Small bleeds may resolve (grade 1 can leave a cystic cavity / small subependymal cyst after the bleed). Mostly good outcome, small ↑ risk of mild delay.

Grade 3

Blood clots and organizes in the aqueduct, 4th-ventricle foramina or arachnoid granulations → post-hemorrhagic hydrocephalus (may need a shunt); developmental delay.

Grade 4

Very severe: high mortality or profound deficits; periventricular hemorrhagic infarction → porencephalic cyst, spastic hemiplegia, epilepsy, ID.

Bleedmatrix → ventricle
→
Clotorganizes in aqueduct / foramina / granulations
→
CSF blockedventricles dilate
→
Hydrocephalus↑ head size, parenchymal compression
  • Survivors of perinatal injury (any lesion): intellectual disability, seizures, and cerebral palsy with ataxia, spasticity and choreoathetosis.
CheckWhere can organized blood block CSF after an IVH? Name three sites.
Cerebral aqueduct, foramina of Luschka/Magendie (4th ventricle outlets), and arachnoid granulations (→ communicating hydrocephalus).
Q2. Why does PVL cause spastic diplegia (legs worse than arms)?
Memory tool

"Legs hug the ventricle." Leg fibers run closest to the lateral ventricle, so periventricular damage hits them first → diplegia (two legs).

Q3. What is the outlook for multicystic encephalopathy and term hypoxic-ischemic injury, and what helps?
  • Multicystic encephalopathy: no specific treatment; death within weeks, months or years. Survivors: microcephaly, spastic quadriplegia, intractable epilepsy, severe ID, cortical blindness, feeding failure (G-tube), aspiration.
  • Perinatal injury overall → death, or ID, seizures and cerebral palsy with spasticity, ataxia and choreoathetosis (basal ganglia/thalamic injury after acute profound term asphyxia).
LesionShort-termLong-termPrevention / treatment
Germinal matrix hemorrhageShock, anemia, apnea, seizures, death (grade 3–4)Post-hemorrhagic hydrocephalus, hemiplegia (grade 4), CP, ID, epilepsyAntenatal steroids, avoid BP swings, delayed cord clamping; serial ultrasound; CSF drainage → VP shunt
PVLOften silentSpastic diplegia, visual impairment, cognitive/attention problemsPrevent preterm birth/infection; antenatal magnesium sulfate lowers CP risk; physiotherapy, botulinum toxin, baclofen
Multicystic encephalopathySeizures, hypertonia, abnormal cry, feeding failureMicrocephaly, quadriplegia, epilepsy, death in weeks–yearsSupportive; therapeutic hypothermia (≥36 wk with moderate-severe HIE, start <6 h) aims to prevent this outcome
CheckName one antenatal drug that reduces IVH and one that reduces CP in preterm infants.
Corticosteroids (betamethasone/dexamethasone) ↓ IVH and RDS. Magnesium sulfate before very preterm delivery ↓ cerebral palsy.
Step 1 HY — Outcome patterns
  • Preterm → PVL → spastic diplegia. Grade 4 IVH → contralateral spastic hemiplegia.
  • Term, acute profound asphyxia → basal ganglia/thalamus → dyskinetic (choreoathetoid) CP.
  • Term, prolonged partial asphyxia → parasagittal watershed cortex → proximal arm/shoulder weakness; severe/global → multicystic encephalopathy → spastic quadriplegia + microcephaly.
  • Hydrocephalus ex vacuo: no shunt needed. Post-hemorrhagic hydrocephalus: shunt.
Step 1 trap

Choreoathetosis after a perinatal insult: if there was severe jaundice, think kernicterus (globus pallidus, subthalamic nucleus); if there was an acute sentinel event at term, think basal ganglia–thalamic HIE. Same movement disorder, different cause.

Buzzwords
"scissoring legs, ex-preemie" → PVL, spastic diplegia "enlarging head after NICU bleed" → post-hemorrhagic hydrocephalus "microcephaly + quadriplegia + seizures from birth" → multicystic encephalopathy "non-progressive motor disorder" → cerebral palsy

ApplyLO 9 application questions

A1An infant born at 25 weeks had a grade 4 hemorrhage on the left. Predict the motor outcome.
Right-sided spastic hemiplegia (contralateral to the left periventricular hemorrhagic infarct), often plus post-hemorrhagic hydrocephalus and epilepsy.
A2A former 28-week preemie, now 8 months old, has a rapidly growing head and a bulging fontanelle. What happened, and what's the treatment?
Post-hemorrhagic hydrocephalus after an IVH (organized clot blocking CSF pathways) → CSF diversion (VP shunt).
A3A term baby with moderate HIE after cord prolapse is 2 hours old. What intervention may prevent multicystic injury?
Therapeutic hypothermia (whole-body cooling to ≈33.5 °C for 72 h), started within 6 hours of birth.
A4A 4-year-old with CP from perinatal asphyxia is losing previously acquired words and motor skills. Does this fit CP?
No. CP is non-progressive; regression points to a neurodegenerative or metabolic disease (e.g., leukodystrophy) and needs a new work-up.

IMGImage ID drillName the lesion before you open the card

1 · Name it
Semilobar / lobar holoprosencephaly: shallow fissure, no corpus callosum, frontal cortex continuous across the midline.
2 · Name it
Lissencephaly type I: thick cortex, thin white matter, smooth surface (LIS1/DCX).
3 · Name it
Subcortical band heterotopia ("double cortex"): female DCX carrier.
4 · Name it
Polymicrogyria: many small gyri, cobblestone/Morocco-leather surface.
5 · Name the cell
Balloon cells → FCD IIb (same picture in tubers and hemimegalencephaly).
6 · Name the tissue
Area medullovasculosa: open, vascular neural plate of a myelomeningocele.
7 · Name it
Multicystic encephalopathy: cysts crossed by a spider's web of gliovascular bands.
8 · Grade each
Top-left 1, top-right 2, bottom-left 3, bottom-right 4 (germinal matrix hemorrhage).

MCQPractice questionsClick an answer to see the explanation.

Score: 0 / 0

1A 27-year-old woman at 17 weeks' gestation has an elevated maternal serum α-fetoprotein. Amniotic fluid shows elevated AFP and acetylcholinesterase. Ultrasound shows an open lumbosacral sac containing neural tissue, scalloped frontal bones and a cerebellum curved around the brainstem. Which additional finding is most likely in this infant after birth?

C. Chiari II malformation. Myelomeningocele (open sac, ↑ AFP/AChE, lemon and banana signs) is accompanied by Chiari II in >95% of cases: small posterior fossa, vermis and medulla through the foramen magnum, aqueductal stenosis → hydrocephalus. A = Dandy-Walker (large posterior fossa). B = holoprosencephaly (not an NTD). D = DCX band heterotopia. E = Chiari I, an adolescent/adult lesion not tied to myelomeningocele.

2A 24-year-old woman with juvenile myoclonic epilepsy well controlled on valproic acid plans to conceive within a year. Her previous pregnancy ended because of anencephaly. Which measure would most reduce the risk of a neural tube defect in her next pregnancy?

A. Valproate impairs folate metabolism and is the highest-risk antiseizure drug for NTDs; switching drugs plus ≈4 mg/day folate (prior NTD + antiepileptic) before conception covers the day 26–28 closure window. B is too low a dose and too late. C prevents hemorrhagic disease of the newborn, not NTDs. D detects but doesn't prevent. E is not the key vitamin and the timing is wrong.

3A newborn has hypotelorism, a single central maxillary incisor and a flat nose with a single nostril. MRI shows partial fusion of the frontal lobes and absence of the corpus callosum. Karyotype is 46,XY. His mother has mild hypotelorism. A defect in which signaling pathway is most likely responsible?

E. Sonic hedgehog. Holoprosencephaly with midline facial defects ("the face predicts the brain") in a child with a normal karyotype and a mildly affected parent fits an inherited SHH mutation with variable expressivity. A and B are general developmental pathways not classically tied to HPE. C (FGFR3) causes achondroplasia. D (reelin) causes lissencephaly with cerebellar hypoplasia.

4A 2-year-old boy has infantile spasms, severe developmental delay and hypotonia. MRI shows a smooth cerebral surface that is most severe in the frontal lobes. His mother has had focal seizures since adolescence, and her MRI shows a continuous band of grey matter deep to a normal-appearing cortex. Which gene is most likely mutated?

B. DCX (doublecortin), X-linked. Hemizygous males → anterior-predominant lissencephaly; heterozygous females → subcortical band heterotopia ("double cortex"). A = LIS1, autosomal dominant and posterior-predominant. C = tuberous sclerosis (tubers, not smooth brain). D = FLNA, periventricular nodular heterotopia. E = RELN, AR lissencephaly with cerebellar hypoplasia.

5A 4-month-old girl has feeding difficulty, hypotonia and frequent seizures. Examination shows microcephaly, bitemporal hollowing, a small jaw and a short nose. MRI shows near-complete agyria, worst in the parieto-occipital regions. Which genetic finding is most likely?

D. 17p13.3 deletion (Miller-Dieker). Loss of LIS1 + neighboring genes → posterior-predominant lissencephaly with characteristic facies. A → holoprosencephaly. B → Angelman (UBE3A): microcephaly, ataxia, happy demeanor, but not agyria. C → DiGeorge/velocardiofacial. E → fragile X (macroorchidism, long face), no lissencephaly.

6A 7-year-old boy has had daily focal seizures since age 3 despite three antiseizure drugs. He has no skin lesions and no family history. MRI shows thickening of one frontal gyrus with a blurred grey–white junction. The lesion is resected. Microscopy shows loss of cortical lamination, large misoriented neurons with clumped Nissl substance, and large cells with glassy eosinophilic cytoplasm and eccentric nuclei. What is the diagnosis?

C. FCD IIb: dyslamination + dysmorphic neurons + balloon cells in a single focal lesion causing drug-resistant epilepsy. Identical histology occurs in tuberous sclerosis tubers, but this child has a single lesion and no other stigmata. A is a tumor with neoplastic ganglion cells and glia (often cystic, temporal). B shows many small gyri, not balloon cells. D arises at the foramen of Monro in TSC. E = neuronal loss and gliosis in CA1 (temporal lobe epilepsy).

7A 9-month-old has clusters of flexor spasms. Examination shows several hypopigmented, leaf-shaped macules on the trunk. Echocardiography shows multiple intracardiac masses. MRI shows multiple cortical lesions with blurring of the grey–white junction and nodules along the lateral ventricles. Loss of function of the affected gene product most directly leads to which of the following?

A. Tuberous sclerosis (ash-leaf spots, cardiac rhabdomyomas, cortical tubers, subependymal nodules, infantile spasms). Hamartin–tuberin (TSC1/TSC2) normally inactivate Rheb; loss → mTORC1 overactivity → cell growth (treated with everolimus). B = NF1. C = von Hippel-Lindau. D = LIS1/DCX lissencephaly. E = holoprosencephaly.

8A boy born at 26 weeks is mechanically ventilated for respiratory distress syndrome. On day 2 he becomes hypotensive and bradycardic; the anterior fontanelle is bulging and the hematocrit has fallen from 46% to 33%. Cranial ultrasound shows echogenic material filling dilated lateral ventricles. Where did the hemorrhage most likely begin?

D. Germinal matrix. In preterm infants (<34 wk) IVH begins in the fragile, stroma-poor capillary bed of the subependymal germinal matrix and ruptures into the ventricle; dilated ventricles make this grade 3. A = subdural (trauma, term/shaken baby). B = choroid plexus bleeds are the typical source of IVH in term infants. C = epidural (skull fracture). E is rare and not linked to prematurity.

9A 2-year-old boy born at 28 weeks after maternal chorioamnionitis cannot walk independently. His legs are spastic with brisk reflexes, bilateral Babinski signs and scissoring; arm function and language are near normal. MRI shows reduced periventricular white matter and irregular lateral ventricles. Which mechanism best explains his condition?

B. Periventricular leukomalacia → spastic diplegia. Leg corticospinal fibers run closest to the ventricles. Preterm periventricular white matter is a watershed, and pre-oligodendrocytes are vulnerable to ischemia, cytokines (chorioamnionitis) and free radicals. A = kernicterus (dyskinetic CP, gaze palsy, deafness). C = a malformation; would show abnormal gyri/heterotopia, not white matter loss. D = tethered cord (LMN signs, bladder). E = focal hemorrhage, unilateral.

10A monochorionic twin pregnancy is complicated by the death of one twin at 33 weeks. The surviving girl is delivered at 36 weeks with seizures, hypertonia, an abnormal cry and microcephaly. She dies at 3 months. At autopsy the brain weighs half of normal; coronal sections show the hemispheres replaced by multiple cavities crossed by fine strands of tissue, and the ventricles are enlarged. Microscopy shows gliosis, calcification and dilated vessels. Which diagnosis is most likely?

E. Multicystic encephalopathy: late-gestation global hypoxic-ischemic necrosis (co-twin death) → liquefaction, cysts with a "spider's web" of gliovascular bands, ventricles enlarged ex vacuo, calcium and gliosis. A is a malformation (no cysts/gliosis, single ventricle). B is a small preterm subependymal bleed. C causes diffuse calcifications and hydrocephalus but not global cystic replacement after a co-twin death. D enlarges ventricles by pressure with an otherwise preserved, large head.

11A 15-year-old girl has 6 months of occipital headaches worsened by coughing, unsteady gait and recent urinary urgency. She has loss of pain and temperature sensation over the shoulders and upper arms bilaterally, with preserved vibration and position sense, and wasting of the hand muscles. Which finding is most likely on MRI?

A. Chiari I with syringomyelia. Cough headache from tonsillar herniation; cape-like loss of pain/temperature with preserved dorsal columns = central cord lesion at the anterior white commissure; anterior horn involvement → hand wasting. B = Dandy-Walker (infancy, hydrocephalus). C = Chiari II (infants, with myelomeningocele). D = PVL. E = tuberous sclerosis.

12A 3-month-old has a tuft of dark hair over the lumbosacral spine. Neurologic examination is normal, and the skin is intact. His mother's prenatal screening was normal. Imaging shows a defect of the L5 posterior vertebral arch with normal meninges and cord. Which of the following best describes this lesion?

C. Spina bifida occulta: mildest NTD, skin closed, normal AFP, often marked by a hair tuft, dimple or lipoma; watch later for tethered cord. A = meningocele. B = myelomeningocele (↑ AFP, deficits). D = anencephaly. E = encephalocele.

13A 31-year-old woman presents in preterm labor at 27 weeks. Delivery appears likely within 24–48 hours. Administration of which drug to the mother now would most reduce the newborn's risk of intraventricular hemorrhage?

B. Antenatal corticosteroids accelerate fetal lung and vascular maturation, reducing RDS, BP instability and germinal matrix/intraventricular hemorrhage. (Magnesium sulfate in the same window reduces cerebral palsy.) A is a tocolytic that can cause premature ductal closure. C prevents vitamin K–deficiency bleeding (given to the newborn). D augments labor. E prevents NTDs only when taken before conception.
